implementation_notes: On the JVM the carrier is a library object rather than language syntax: grpc-java's Context.withDeadline(deadline, scheduler) creates a CancellableContext that cancels itself at the deadline and cascades cancellation to descendants, while getDeadline() exposes the absolute deadline and cancellationCause() records why it fired. A hop runs its work inside the context (run/call) so outgoing RPCs inherit the deadline - grpc-java propagates it by default, which makes this the canonical realization - and cancels the context in a finally block so it can be collected. The classic per-stage Future.get(timeout) arrangement is replaced by the scoped context. Sibling variant: without an RPC framework the budget is split by hand over CompletableFuture.orTimeout/completeOnTimeout against one nanoTime-based deadline.
pitfalls: Every attach() needs a matching detach() and every CancellableContext a cancel(); the javadoc states that breaking these rules leaks memory.
Context is scoped to the current thread: work handed to another thread must be wrapped (wrap(Runnable), currentContextExecutor) or the deadline and cancellation do not follow.
withDeadline cancels the context but cannot stop code that ignores isCancelled(); long computations must check the context at stage boundaries.
Do not compute the budget from System.currentTimeMillis(); the deadline is scheduled on the system nano clock, so treat getDeadline() as authoritative and derive remaining time consistently.

variants.name: CompletableFuture.orTimeout per stage over one shared deadline (JDK)
variants.implementation_notes: Without an RPC framework there is no ambient context, so the budget must be split by hand: keep one absolute deadlineNanos (System.nanoTime based) and give each asynchronous stage CompletableFuture.orTimeout(remaining, unit) - exceptionally completing it with TimeoutException when the budget runs out - or completeOnTimeout for a fallback value. The class maintains a single daemon thread for delays and timeouts, so the mechanism is cheap, but it is per-future: the hop must recompute remaining at every stage and must not hand a stage a fresh full timeout. It composes naturally with allOf/anyOf fan-outs, one orTimeout per child.
pitfalls: orTimeout completes the future exceptionally but does not cancel the underlying work (no thread interruption); the producer continues unless it observes cancellation itself.
Chaining orTimeout per stage with a fresh constant turns the budget into a sum again - always derive from the one deadlineNanos.
CancellationException from CompletableFuture.cancel() is not TimeoutException; if explicit cancel is used on expiry, handle both paths.
join() wraps failures in CompletionException, so unwrap the cause before mapping to a deadline error or the real cause is lost.
